svg.title: the framework repairs its own GitLab setup when something breaks it: init heals a revoked, duplicate, wrong or weakened token and an unguarded variable, and reload puts a drifted project back
svg.text: the framework repairs its own GitLab setup when something
Scenario: init heals a revoked, duplicate, wrong or weakened token and an unguarded variable, and reload puts a
A revoked release token is rebuilt
A duplicate token and a tampered variable are repaired
A variable that signs in as another token is fixed
A release token that cannot push is rebuilt
A variable that lost its guards gets them back, with the same token
A project that drifted is put back in one command

g.text: Given a project the framework set up, whose release token someone then revoked in GitLab
GitLab's access-tokens page of a project after its first `task devsecops:init`. That run created two tokens, the release
token TASK_COMMITIZEN_TOKEN and the dependency robot's TASK_RENOVATE_TOKEN.
Someone has since revoked the release token in GitLab. "Active project access tokens" lists only TASK_RENOVATE_TOKEN,
and the release token sits under "Inactive project access tokens", marked "Revoked". Dates, last use and expiry change
on every run, so they are blanked.
When the developer runs the framework's init again, a brand-new release token takes the
revoked one's place
The developer runs `task devsecops:init` again. "Active project access tokens" lists TASK_COMMITIZEN_TOKEN once more: a
new token, while the old one stays below, still "Revoked".
The same run stored the new token in the CI/CD variable of the same name. The test checks that this variable, like the
dependency robot's, signs in to GitLab as its own active token.
When the developer runs init a second time, GitLab keeps that release token and revokes
nothing
A second `task devsecops:init` on the healed project. The page has not changed: the same release token is active, and
"Inactive project access tokens" still holds one row. The init run found a working token and left it alone.
When someone plants a second release token with the same name in GitLab
The same project. Someone creates a second token named TASK_COMMITIZEN_TOKEN in GitLab, so "Active project access
tokens" now lists two release tokens where there should be one.
And someone overwrites the release token's CI/CD variable with a bad value
Someone also overwrites the release token's CI/CD variable. The project's CI/CD settings, values revealed (the button
now reads "Hide values"): TASK_COMMITIZEN_TOKEN now holds "tampered-by-e2e", which no pipeline can sign in with.
TASK_RENOVATE_TOKEN still holds a real token. It starts with "glpat-" like every GitLab token, and its secret part is
masked as "*****".
When the developer runs the framework's init once more, a single release token is left
One more `task devsecops:init`. "Active project access tokens" lists a single release token again, and "Inactive project
access tokens" now holds three.
The first is the token revoked in chapter 1. The second is the older of the two duplicates, which the init run revoked.
The third is the one it kept, which it then replaced with a new token because the CI/CD variable no longer matched it.
Then the CI/CD variable holds a GitLab token again instead of the bad value
The same CI/CD settings page, values revealed. TASK_COMMITIZEN_TOKEN holds a GitLab token again, "glpat-" with its
secret part masked, where it held "tampered-by-e2e". The test checks that this value signs in to GitLab as the new
release token.
When someone pastes the dependency robot's token into the release token's CI/CD variable
The same CI/CD settings, values revealed. Someone pasted the dependency robot's token into the release token's variable,
so TASK_COMMITIZEN_TOKEN and TASK_RENOVATE_TOKEN now hold the same value.
Nothing on this page gives it away. Both read "glpat-*****" and both keep their "Protected" and "Masked" badges, because
the value is a real token that signs in to GitLab. The test checks that it signs in as the dependency robot's token, not
as the release token.
When the developer runs init again, it replaces the release token the variable did not sign
in as
One more `task devsecops:init`. It asks GitLab which token the variable signs in as. The answer is not the release
token, so init replaced the release token with a new one and stored that one in the variable.
"Inactive project access tokens" now counts 4: the replaced release token joined the three from chapters 1 and 2.
TASK_RENOVATE_TOKEN is still the same token, and the test checks that each variable signs in as its own token again.
When someone swaps the release token for one that cannot push to the repository
Someone revoked the release token, made a new TASK_COMMITIZEN_TOKEN by hand and stored it in the variable. Its "Scopes"
column reads only "api". It lacks "write_repository", the right to push to the repository, which the release job needs.
"Inactive project access tokens" counts 5 with the token revoked by hand. The new token signs in and the variable holds
it, so only its scopes give it away.
When the developer runs init again, the release token can push to the repository again
One more `task devsecops:init`. It compared the token's scopes with the ones it needs, revoked the hand-made token and
created a new one. The active TASK_COMMITIZEN_TOKEN reads "api, write_repository" again, and "Inactive project access
tokens" counts 6, with the hand-made token, the row that reads only "api", among them.
The same run stored the new token in the CI/CD variable. The test checks that the variable signs in as it.
When someone turns masking off on the release token's CI/CD variable
The CI/CD settings again. Someone turned masking off on TASK_COMMITIZEN_TOKEN. Under its name the "Masked" badge is
gone, and only "Protected" and "Expanded" are left. Masked means GitLab hides the value in every job log.
And someone turns protection off on that variable as well
Someone also turned protection off. Only "Expanded" is left under TASK_COMMITIZEN_TOKEN. Protected means only pipelines
on protected branches, such as the main branch, can read the value.
When the developer runs init again, the variable is masked and protected again
One more `task devsecops:init`. TASK_COMMITIZEN_TOKEN shows "Protected" and "Masked" again, like TASK_RENOVATE_TOKEN
below it. Its value still reads "glpat-*****", and the test checks that it is the very same token as before.
Then GitLab still lists the same release token, because init replaced nothing
The access-tokens page after that run looks exactly as it did at the end of the previous chapter: one active release
token, and "Inactive project access tokens" still counts 6. The token was right, so init fixed the variable's settings
and replaced nothing.
Given a project the framework set up, whose main branch someone then loosened by hand
A new project, generated from the toolbox and set up on install day. Its repository settings, "Protected branches": the
main branch says "Allowed to push and merge: Maintainers".
The toolbox sets that to "No one", so every change reaches the main branch through a merge request. Someone loosened it
by hand.
And the project added its own settings to .env.dist, .env.dev, the MegaLinter settings and
the Trivy ignore list
Four files hold a few lines from the toolbox and everything else from the project: .env.dist, .env.dev, the MegaLinter
settings .config/megalinter/config.yml and the Trivy ignore list .config/trivy/trivyignore.yml.
GitLab's page for the commit "chore: add the project's own settings": four changed files, with one green line of the
project's own added at the end of each.

text.tspan: git commit -am "chore: add the project's own settings" && git push origin main

g.text: And someone pushed a hand edit of the pipeline file straight to the main branch
That loosening lets someone push a hand edit straight to the main branch. GitLab's page for the commit "chore: tweak the
pipeline by hand": one changed file, .gitlab-ci.yml, with one green line added at its end, "# a hand-edited line the
toolbox never wrote".

text.tspan: git commit -am "chore: tweak the pipeline by hand" && git push origin main

g.text: When the developer reloads the framework, both automation tokens are revoked and replaced by
new ones
The developer runs `task devsecops:reload`. It re-applies the project's own answers to the framework files, then redoes
the GitLab setup. On the access-tokens page both tokens are active, and both install-day tokens sit under "Inactive
project access tokens", marked "Revoked".
The reload replaced them even though they still worked, and stored each new token in its CI/CD variable. `task
devsecops:init` never replaces a working token, as chapters 1 and 5 showed.
Then the main branch is locked down again
The same "Protected branches" settings as before the reload. The main branch says "Allowed to push and merge: No one"
again, and "Allowed to merge: Maintainers": a change now reaches the main branch only through a merge request.
And the developer sends the restored pipeline file back through a merge request
The reload also put .gitlab-ci.yml back on disk, without the hand-written line. The main branch is locked, so the
developer commits it on a branch and opens a merge request with the push.
GitLab's page for that commit, the same kind of page as the hand edit: "1 merge request", one changed file,
.gitlab-ci.yml, and the red line "# a hand-edited line the toolbox never wrote" removed.
The four files with the project's own settings are not in the commit: the reload left those lines where the project put
them.

text.tspan: git switch -c reload-framework && git commit -am "chore: put the framework files back" && git push -o
